title: Advanced Cartography and Spatial Analysis
description: Master advanced cartographic and spatial analysis skills.
objectives: Create and interpret choropleth and other thematic maps
Apply spatial analysis using data
Evaluate cartographic choices and their biases

lessons.title: Cartographic Choices and Bias
lessons.content: Every map reflects choices — and those choices shape how we see the world.
examples: Mercator projection: standard for navigation but makes tropical countries look small
'North up' convention: arbitrary but makes northern hemisphere seem 'on top' psychologically
Color choices: sequential (light→dark) vs. diverging (two colors from center) scales imply different things

lessons.title: Spatial Analysis
lessons.content: Spatial analysis finds patterns and relationships in geographic data.
examples: Spatial autocorrelation: are nearby things more similar than distant things? (Tobler's First Law: everything is related, but nearby things more so)
Hotspot analysis: cluster of high values surrounded by other high values
Spatial interpolation: estimate values between measured points (e.g., rainfall between weather stations)

title: Physical Geography — Advanced Systems
description: Advanced study of Earth's physical systems and their interactions.
objectives: Analyze feedback loops in Earth's climate system
Apply systems thinking to physical geography
Model a geographic process

lessons.title: Climate Feedback Loops
lessons.content: Feedback loops amplify or dampen climate change.
examples: Ice-albedo feedback: warming melts ice → less white surface to reflect sunlight → more warming (positive/amplifying feedback)
Water vapor feedback: warming → more evaporation → more water vapor (greenhouse gas) → more warming
Permafrost feedback: warming → permafrost thaws → releases methane → more warming
Only major negative feedback: more clouds might increase reflection, but this is uncertain

lessons.title: Earth as a System
lessons.content: All of Earth's systems are interconnected in complex ways.
examples: The carbon cycle links the lithosphere (rock weathering), hydrosphere (ocean absorption), biosphere (photosynthesis), and atmosphere (CO₂)
ENSO connects Pacific Ocean temperatures to rainfall on six continents
A forest can create its own rainfall through transpiration — clear the forest and the rainfall may stop (Amazon tipping point)

title: Human-Environment Interaction — Deep Analysis
description: Analyze human-environment interactions across history and into the future.
objectives: Apply the concept of the Anthropocene
Analyze planetary boundaries
Evaluate the transition to sustainable development

lessons.title: The Anthropocene
lessons.content: Geologists propose we have entered a new epoch defined by human impact on Earth's systems.
examples: Proposed start: 1950s (nuclear bomb testing left permanent radioactive markers in rock)
Signatures: plastics in ocean sediments, atmospheric CO₂, mass extinction, novel ecosystems
Humans now move more rock and sediment annually than all natural geological processes combined

lessons.title: Planetary Boundaries
lessons.content: Scientists have identified nine boundaries; crossing them risks catastrophic, irreversible change.
examples: Boundaries already crossed: climate change, biodiversity loss, land-system change, novel entities (chemicals/plastics)
Boundaries at risk: freshwater, ocean acidification, nitrogen cycle
Still within safe range: ozone, aerosol loading, atmospheric aerosols

title: Geopolitics — Advanced
description: Advanced study of geopolitics, international relations, and geographic power.
objectives: Apply major geopolitical theories
Analyze contemporary geopolitical conflicts
Evaluate the future of the international order

lessons.title: Geopolitical Theories
lessons.content: Geographic theories help explain international power dynamics.
examples: Mackinder's Heartland (1904): control central Eurasia → control the world; influenced Cold War strategy
Spykman's Rimland (1942): Eurasia's coastal 'rim' is more important than the interior — influenced NATO strategy
Brzezinski's Grand Chessboard (1997): Eurasia is the 'grand chessboard' for 21st-century power

lessons.title: Contemporary Geopolitics
lessons.content: The post-Cold War unipolar moment is ending; a multipolar world is emerging.
examples: China's rise: 'Indo-Pacific' replacing 'Asia-Pacific' in U.S. strategic thinking
BRICS expansion: Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa + Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, UAE, Saudi Arabia
Arctic geopolitics: Russia has most Arctic territory; Canada, Norway, Denmark, U.S. also claim — importance growing as ice melts

title: Economic Geography — Globalization and Finance
description: Analyze the financial geography of globalization and the future of work.
objectives: Map global financial flows
Analyze the geography of offshore finance
Evaluate the future of work in a globalized economy

lessons.title: Financial Geography
lessons.content: Finance is highly concentrated but globally connected.
examples: Global financial centers: New York (1), London (2), Singapore (3), Hong Kong (4)
Offshore finance: Cayman Islands, British Virgin Islands, Luxembourg — trillions held to minimize tax
Global remittances: migrants send $800 billion/year to home countries — exceeds global foreign aid

lessons.title: Future of Work
lessons.content: Globalization and automation are restructuring the geography of work.
examples: Offshoring: jobs moved to low-wage countries (manufacturing to China; call centers to India, Philippines)
Reshoring: rising wages in China + automation + supply chain concerns → some manufacturing returning
AI automation: repetitive white-collar work (accounting, legal research, data entry) increasingly automated
Remote work: COVID showed many knowledge workers can work from anywhere — changing geography of cities

title: Environmental Geography — Advanced
description: Advanced analysis of environmental geography and the transition to sustainability.
objectives: Apply political ecology to environmental issues
Analyze environmental justice cases
Evaluate pathways to sustainable development

lessons.title: Political Ecology
lessons.content: Environmental problems reflect power relationships — who decides who bears environmental burdens?
examples: Environmental justice: communities of color and low-income communities bear disproportionate pollution burdens (e.g., Cancer Alley, Louisiana)
Climate justice: countries that emitted least (Pacific Islands, sub-Saharan Africa) suffer most from climate change
Water privatization: when water is sold to the highest bidder, the poor lose access

title: Urban Geography — Global Cities
description: Study global city systems, urban inequality, and future urban challenges.
objectives: Apply global city theory
Analyze urban inequality using the Gini coefficient
Evaluate smart city and urban resilience strategies

lessons.title: Global City Theory
lessons.content: Certain cities function as command centers of the global economy.
examples: Saskia Sassen's 'global cities' (1991): New York, London, Tokyo — where global finance, law, and consulting are concentrated
Alpha++ cities (GaWC ranking): London and New York lead
Global cities attract talent and capital but generate extreme inequality

title: Regional Geography — Europe and Russia
description: Advanced study of European and Russian geography.
objectives: Analyze Russia's geography and geopolitical behavior
Describe post-communist transformation of Eastern Europe
Evaluate EU geography and politics

lessons.title: Russia's Geography
lessons.content: Russia's vast geography shapes its history, economy, and geopolitics.
examples: Largest country by area (17 million km²); spans 11 time zones
Landlocked problem: limited warm-water port access drives historic expansion toward Black Sea, Baltic, Pacific
Resource wealth: world's largest natural gas reserves; top oil producer; huge mineral wealth
Harsh climate: 65% of territory is permafrost; growing season limited to a few months

title: Geography of Conflict and Peacebuilding
description: Apply geographic analysis to understand conflict and peacebuilding.
objectives: Map current global conflicts and their geographic causes
Analyze geographic factors in post-conflict reconstruction
Evaluate geographic approaches to peacebuilding

lessons.title: Geography of Conflict
examples: Resource wars: DRC (coltan, gold, diamonds), South Sudan (oil), Niger Delta (oil) — resource wealth funds and incentivizes conflict
Border disputes: South China Sea (overlapping maritime claims), Kashmir (three nuclear powers)
Climate-conflict link: research shows each 1°C of warming increases risk of civil conflict by ~6%

lessons.title: Peacebuilding Geography
examples: Divided cities: Nicosia (Cyprus) — last divided capital in Europe; Mostar (Bosnia); Belfast (Northern Ireland)
Post-conflict resource management: Liberia's timber ban removed the economic motive for conflict
Cross-border cooperation: transboundary water management (Mekong River Commission) can build peace or trigger conflict

title: Geography of the Future
description: Apply geographic thinking to anticipate and shape the future world.
objectives: Develop scenarios for future geographic change
Evaluate the geographic dimensions of emerging technologies
Apply geographic reasoning to long-term challenges

lessons.title: Future Scenarios
lessons.content: Geographers use scenario planning to prepare for different futures.
examples: Climate scenario RCP 8.5 (business as usual): ~4°C warming by 2100 — most of tropics become uninhabitable in summer
RCP 2.6 (aggressive action): ~1.5°C warming — still serious but manageable
Population scenarios: UN medium scenario: 10.4 billion by 2100; high scenario: 15.9 billion
The world you inherit in 2050 depends largely on decisions made in the next 10 years

lessons.title: Your Geographic Agency
lessons.content: Geography is not destiny — you can shape the future.
examples: Vote in local elections — zoning, transportation, and land use are decided locally
Consumer choices: where things are made and how they're transported has geographic consequences
Career: geography-related careers growing: GIS analyst, urban planner, climate scientist, development economist, epidemiologist
The world's greatest challenges (climate, inequality, conflict, pandemics) are fundamentally geographic problems that need geographically-informed solutions
